newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler sees continued incentive spending.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler sees continued incentive spending.

text.p: Chrysler Corp Chief Financial officer Gary Valade said Friday that he expects the automaker's incentive spending to remain at its current level of $1,195 per vehicle during the July and August clearance of 1997 models.

Valade, speaking to reporters in a conference call following distribution of Chrysler's second quarter earnings, said he expects the U.S. automotive market to remain fiercely competitive, although industry sales should remain in the 15 million to 15.5 million range for the full year.

Valade said the sales levels have required more incentive support than anticipated. Chrysler's incentive rose to a second quarter average of $980 per vehicle, ending the period at $1,195. Incentives averaged $625 in the second quarter of 1996

"We think sales are going to continue in the 15-15.5 million unit range," Valade said "The thing I'd say about it is that it's somewhat more levitated by incentives than we thought when we projected it."

The incentives, along with a 29-day engine plant strike that cost Chrysler about 89,000 trucks, held the automaker's second quarter net income to $483 million, or $0.70 a share, down 53 percent from a year ago.

But Valade said he believes Chrysler dealt with its adversity well, maintaining positive operating cash flow and allowing its automotive cash balance after dividends and stock repurchases to fall only to $7.04 billion from $7.62 billion at the end of the first quarter.
He called the quarter a "dry run" for Chrysler's ability to weather an industry downturn because its shipments were down 20 percent from the company's initial plans for the quarter.
"It's equivalent to having a 20 percent downturn in one quarter," Valade said. "And we were able to react very well-- more quickly than we had anticipated."
Chrysler's second quarter factory shipments of 738,453 vehicles were down 7.9 percent from last year's 801,769 units.

The automaker has taken austerity measures, including instituting a hiring freeze, reducing overtime and travel and cutting reducing discretionary capital expenditures. The company also is working to reduce warranty expenses.
Valade said the company has set an internal target of cutting non-product-related capital spending by $1 billion over the next 12 months.
"We're still working on it. We've had an informal target of $1 billion over probably the next 12 months," Valade said. "I don't know if we'll get to that level or not, but that was the target."
He said the cutbacks will not alter Chrysler's decision-making process for a new plant to replace its 87-year-old Toledo, Ohio, assembly plant.
